meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If my critics saw me walking over the River Thames they would say it was because I couldn't swim'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote files this under Misattributed: it is a reworked Lyndon Johnson line about the Potomac, moved to the Thames.

answer.label: Not Thatcher — an adapted Lyndon Johnson line
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this under Misattributed ↗ for Thatcher and identifies it as an adapted Lyndon Johnson quote: “If one morning I walked on top of the water across the Potomac River, the headline that afternoon would read: ‘President Can’t Swim.’” Be aware of the limit of that finding: we could not reach the newspaper article Wikiquote names as the source of the Thatcher attribution, and we found no primary source — no transcript, no contemporary report — for the Johnson original either. The one thing well supported here is the negative: this is not a documented Thatcher line.

source.excerpt: If one morning I walked on top of the water across the Potomac River, the headline that afternoon would read: ‘President Can’t Swim.’
trail: Wikiquote ↗ states that the Thames version is “actually an adapted Lyndon Johnson quote” and prints the Potomac wording in full. That is the anchor for this page.
The Daily Telegraph feature Wikiquote cites as the source of the Thatcher attribution is on a host this run could not reach, so we cannot say what it claims beyond Wikiquote’s summary of it.

We searched Quote Investigator for the Potomac wording and for “President Can’t Swim” and found no investigation of either — the specialists have not traced this one, so there is no earlier or firmer finding for us to defer to.

Searches for the Johnson original returned only quotation-aggregator sites, which repeat each other and cite nothing. We have therefore not asserted a date, occasion or publication for it, and this page claims none.
source.excerptNote: This is the wording Wikiquote gives for the Johnson original. We reproduce it as Wikiquote states it; we were not able to confirm it against a speech text, press-conference transcript or contemporary newspaper report.

source.rightsNote: We could not identify the work in which either version was first published, so we assert no rights status. If the Johnson line is genuine it would date from the 1960s and be well inside copyright; that is a reasonable inference, not a verified fact, and we have not built anything on it.

author.name: Lyndon B. Johnson
author.heading: About Lyndon B. Johnson
author.bio: Lyndon Baines Johnson (1908–1973) was the 36th President of the United States, taking office on the assassination of John F. Kennedy in 1963. He had a long and combative relationship with the Washington press corps, which is the soil this particular joke grows in — though we could not find a primary record of him telling it.

misattribution.intro: A stock political joke about walking on water, relocated from Washington to Westminster.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ places the line in its Misattributed section, notes the attribution comes via a newspaper feature and “other sources,” and identifies the real ancestor as a Lyndon Johnson line about the Potomac.

misattribution.truthLine: The shape of the joke — walk on water, get a hostile headline — belongs to Lyndon Johnson ↗ and the Potomac. Whether Thatcher ever repeated it about the Thames is undocumented; whether Johnson ever said it is, on the evidence we could reach, also undocumented.
